still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month, still printed on branded boxes, and almost nobody pays it. Branded injectable semaglutide is now mostly a commercial-formulary and brand-loyalty product.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed at the FDA's request in January 2026 is still off the Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels. The finalised 503B compounding exclusion from April 2026 still stands.
The FDA's July 2028 class bone and lean-mass warning is still on every incretin label, and CMS still pays for DXA scans for incretin users aged 65 and over.
Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums still stands. The September 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing wellness premium differentials of up to 30% is still in force in states without a ban.
Tirzepatide still has no US generic, and its exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32. Its August 2028 dementia-risk label still stands while the required confirmatory trial enrols.

population.note: FICTIONAL estimates. Off-drug arithmetic: 29.5% ever-used minus 22.0% current = 7.5% of adults who used the drugs and are off now. Cycling: 44% of ever-users is 13.0 points. About 10.6 points are current users on at least their second course (~48% of current users), and ~2.4 points are cyclers who are off again. The remaining ~5.1 off-now points stopped once and stayed off. This fits roughly one-third one-year persistence, with restarts rising toward the top of the 36–47% range now that a restart costs $0–69. User count: 22.0% of ~267M adults = ~58.7M current users. Age check: band shares (~20/33/24/23% of adults) × band rates (12/21.5/33/20) ≈ 22.0. FICTIONAL payer mix at end-2030: Medicare ~12.0M (20%), of which ~4.5M are on the new generic obesity benefit and ~7.5M are covered under diabetes, cardiovascular, CKD, sleep-apnoea or dementia codes. About 10.5M of the Medicare users are 65+ (plus ~0.4M aged 65+ paying cash or covered by retiree plans) and ~1.5M are under-65 disability beneficiaries. Medicaid ~8.5M (14.5%). The HRSA free-provision programme covers ~1.5M (2.6%). Public payers total ~22.0M (37.5%), the largest single payer category. Commercial ~15.5M (26.4%). Legitimate cash ~19.7M (33.6%), mostly generic semaglutide at $39–69. Gray market ~1.5M (2.6%), now mainly tirzepatide and retatrutide 'research peptides' rather than semaglutide. Sum 58.7M. More than half of 2030 new starts were publicly paid. The bottom third rose fastest (11% → 19%) through Medicaid opt-ins and free provision, but it still sits below the national figure. Adult obesity is ~33.0%. About one in six adults with obesity has never used a drug. These are mostly working uninsured above the free programme's 250% FPL cut-off, people in the 16 non-covering Medicaid states, and a growing 'unmedicated by choice' minority, which polls put at ~3% of adults. Under-18 use is concentrated at ages 12–17. Medicaid EPSDT obligations brought low-income adolescents in once generics made coverage cheap, which narrowed but did not close the upper-income lead.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. The Metabolic Health Access Act (Nov 2029, in a year-end health package) did three things. (1) Medicare: it created a Part D obesity benefit, effective Mar 2030, limited to generic/AB-rated semaglutide and lowest-net-cost orals, with a $10 copay. Branded tirzepatide stays reachable only through existing codes and prior authorisation. Arithmetic: ~4.5M enrollees by Dec 2030 × ~$55 net/month × 12 ≈ $3.0B annualised. CBO scored $46B over 2030–2039, assuming an average ~7M enrollees × $55 × 12 ≈ $4.6B/yr. That is far below the 2027 $41B score for a branded benefit with a smaller population, because generic prices arrived. (2) Medicaid: it pays a 90% federal match for generic incretins prescribed for obesity. By end-2030, 34 states plus DC cover them, up from 9. Arithmetic: ~8.5M users × ~$55 blended net × 12 ≈ $5.6B/yr total, ~$5.0B federal. Two states still tie continued coverage to adherence and BMI progress at 6 and 12 months. (3) HRSA free provision: generic semaglutide is supplied free through community health centres to uninsured adults under 250% FPL, from Apr 2030. Arithmetic: ~1.5M patients × $32/month federal bulk price × 12 ≈ $0.58B annualised, against a $0.9B annual appropriation that includes distribution and clinic visits.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide costs $5–30/month across 70+ brands. Canadian generics are CAD 45–80. Generics are sold in roughly 175 countries. Indian API makers now also supply several US ANDA holders, so the same molecule that was seized in the mail in 2028 now arrives legally in bulk. Generic liraglutide is near-free in most markets.
access.note: FICTIONAL. The price collapse runs through one mechanism. Under the May 2029 settlement of Paragraph IV litigation, generic semaglutide could enter the US from Jan 2030, and Novo launched an authorised generic the same month. By Q3 2030, generic injectable semaglutide pens cost $39–59/month cash at Cost Plus, Amazon Pharmacy, Walmart and Costco. Generic oral semaglutide costs more, $69–99, because a 25 mg daily tablet needs ~75× the API of a weekly 2.4 mg injection. As a result, public programmes default to the cheaper pen even though the pill now matches it. Branded prices: Lilly cut Foundayo (orforglipron) cash to $99–149 to compete. Zepbound via TrumpRx and LillyDirect is $299–449. Retatrutide is $599–899 cash and rarely covered. Oral amycretin launched Q4 2030 at a $499 cash introductory price. Employer coverage rebounded from 44% to 51% because generic-first step therapy made the benefit cheap; most plans require 3 months of generic semaglutide before a branded drug. About 7% of employers keep monitored metabolic tracks. The gray market shrank by half because semaglutide is no longer worth smuggling. It persists for tirzepatide and retatrutide, sold as 'research peptides' from Chinese suppliers.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, plus generic and authorised-generic semaglutide from Jan 2030)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg, Rybelsus, generic oral semaglutide from 2030)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular agonist, daily oral (oral amycretin, approved Sep 2030)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Mar 2029)
Glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Sep 2029)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established cardiovascular disease (tirzepatide, Aug 2028; confirmatory trial enrolling)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol reduction: still off-label; oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 read out positive in 2030 and the sNDA was filed Oct 2030, with no approval this window
'calm', 'focus' and 'craving freedom': low-dose generic semaglutide sold through telehealth subscriptions as a wellness service
dementia-prevention use by people without cardiovascular disease, now mostly on cheap generic semaglutide rather than tirzepatide, despite EVOKE
nicotine, gambling and compulsive-shopping reduction: observational support, no approvals
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: No new indications arrived this window. Retatrutide was approved in Mar 2029 at its extended decision date, for BMI ≥35 or ≥30 with comorbidity. It carries a dysesthesia warning, and its ~26% mean loss at the top dose is the class best. Uptake is limited by price and a high discontinuation rate. Survodutide was approved in Sep 2029 for obesity; its MASH sNDA is pending and uptake is niche. The oral-parity driver was already partly met by the 2027 Wegovy pill result. This step realises it fully through oral amycretin. Novo filed in Feb 2029 on a phase 3 programme that included a 72-week head-to-head against tirzepatide 15 mg (~20.6% vs ~21.0%, non-inferior). The FDA approved it in Sep 2030, 19 months after filing, and it launched in Q4 2030. A pill now matches the leading injectable class except retatrutide. MariTide (monthly) was filed in Jul 2030, with a decision no earlier than mid-2031. Bimagrumab-type muscle-preserving adjuncts are still in phase 3 and none is approved, despite pressure from the bone warning. The global incretin market is ~$131B (2029). Revenue growth is now almost entirely branded next-generation drugs, and semaglutide is a commodity.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Oral amycretin has a GI profile similar to tirzepatide, with more early nausea. Retatrutide's GI discontinuation is the highest in the class.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; higher absolute rates on retatrutide.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low. MDL settlements concluded in 2029 without admission.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Hip-fracture HR ~1.3 among users aged 65+ after more than 2 years, replicated in a 2030 VA cohort (HR ~1.25). Generic-era expansion has put ~4.5M more older adults on semaglutide under the Medicare benefit, so fracture numbers are expected to rise in absolute terms even if the per-person risk is unchanged. Risk remains concentrated in older women, people with low protein intake and repeated cyclers.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The July 2028 class warning stands. The Medicare obesity benefit requires a baseline DXA for enrollees 65+, and CMS pays for a 12-month repeat. A muscle-preserving adjunct is not yet approved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts are still conflicting; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA lists it under adverse reactions without a class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal, including in the anhedonia analyses.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening (anhedonia, reduced pleasure)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The FDA-requested postmarketing study (n≈61k) and a pooled reanalysis of trials that collected SHAPS data found clinically meaningful anhedonia in ~6.5% of users versus ~2.9% of matched controls. That is an excess of ~3.6 points, roughly one additional affected user in 28. The effect is dose-related, higher on tirzepatide and retatrutide top doses, and reverses in most people within 8–12 weeks of dose reduction or stopping. Milder self-reported 'evenness' is reported by ~30% of users and is not counted as an adverse effect.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Oct 2029 class labelling change: 'reduced pleasure or interest (anhedonia)' added to Warnings and Precautions with the prevalence estimate, plus counselling to report mood changes and consider dose reduction. A Medication Guide paragraph is required with every fill. There is no boxed warning. The FTC and FDA issued warning letters to telehealth firms that market the effect as a benefit.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months, worse after repeated cycles and disproportionately as fat. Cheap restarts have shortened gaps between courses but not reduced the number of courses.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. It underpins chronic-therapy framing, and the two Medicaid programmes that require adherence cite it.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron and vitamin D deficiency case series continue to grow, especially among unsupervised low-dose 'calm' subscribers who see a clinician only through an app.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance only. The HRSA programme bundles a multivitamin and an annual blood panel.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About eight years of follow-up exists for semaglutide and ~1.5 years for retatrutide. Medicaid EPSDT coverage has roughly doubled adolescent use with no peak-bone-mass data; the first pediatric DXA readouts are due 2031.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone-density postmarketing requirements on the oral adolescent approval and on generic labels by reference.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Semaglutide counterfeit reports fell sharply in 2030 as generics undercut them. Harms have shifted to 'research peptide' tirzepatide and retatrutide vials (~2,100 adverse-event reports in 2030), and to substitution confusion when pharmacies switch patients between generic pen makers with different click-to-dose devices.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA import alert still covers unapproved incretins, including retatrutide. FDA device-labelling guidance on generic pen dose markings. State actions against peptide 'research use only' sellers.

safety_ledger.effect: Dysesthesia (skin sensitivity, tingling) with triple agonism
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reported in ~9–20% of retatrutide users at higher doses. Mostly mild, but it is a leading driver of retatrutide discontinuation.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled warning on retatrutide at approval (Mar 2029).

food_and_beverage.state: About 38% of US households now have a user, with the fastest growth in lower-income households, which had been the snack industry's most loyal volume. Snack and confectionery volumes are down ~8–10% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~8%. Price increases no longer fully offset this, and category dollar sales fell ~2% in 2030. Dollar stores and SNAP-heavy grocers report the sharpest shifts. PepsiCo and Mondelez closed two US snack plants. Protein, fibre and small-pack lines are still growing, and private label has taken 'GLP-1 friendly' over.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down ~11% from 2025 and beer ~7%. Most of the loss comes from heavy drinkers on drugs as cheap generics spread the alcohol-reduction effect beyond the insured. Non-alcoholic lines are now ~6% of beer volume. Brown-Forman and Constellation have cut US headcount. Rural and mid-sized-city taverns are closing fastest.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat and checks are smaller. Chains have made small-plate menus permanent. A niche of 'long table' independent restaurants and supper clubs, tied to the unmedicated movement, is growing in Pittsburgh, Asheville and Brooklyn; its fixed-price multi-course nights sell out. Buffets keep closing.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking. Torrid has closed roughly half its 2024 stores. Mainstream brands design for a 'cycling' customer: stretch fabrics, adjustable waists and size-swap programmes. The unmedicated movement has a small apparel aesthetic of loose linen, aprons and 'Born Hungry' slogan shirts.

fitness.state: Strength training keeps growing. The Medicare benefit's DXA requirement has brought body-composition scanning into pharmacies: CVS and Walgreens run DXA kiosks in ~1,200 stores. Community-centre strength classes for adults 65+ are funded by Medicare Advantage plans.

insurance.state: With generic-first step therapy, the cost per covered member for weight management fell ~60%, and employer coverage rose back to 51%. Pharmacy trend moderated to ~+5% in 2030. Branded next-generation drugs sit behind prior authorisation. Adherence-conditioned premiums persist at some large self-insured employers outside Illinois, but they matter less now that the drug costs $40. Medicare Advantage plans compete on 'metabolic' extras.

pharma.state: Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell ~45% in 2030 under generics and its authorised generic, and Novo has cut ~4,000 roles globally. Lilly grows on tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo and is the most valuable healthcare company in the world. Viatris, Teva, Sandoz and Indian ANDA holders split a high-volume, low-margin generic semaglutide market. Oral amycretin is Novo's bid to return to premium pricing.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Lean no longer signals money, because a $40 pen has made it cheap. What signals money now is muscle on a lean frame, a DXA printout on the fridge, and a branded drug name: 'I'm on reta' versus 'I'm on the generic'. A soft, heavy body in a young adult increasingly reads as a choice, and sometimes as a statement.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The price gap has become an efficacy and supervision gap. Public and generic users lose ~13–15% on semaglutide with a ten-minute clinic visit. Commercially insured and cash-rich users get tirzepatide, retatrutide or oral amycretin (~20–26%) plus protein coaching and strength trainers. Older Medicare enrollees are the newest mass cohort and the most fracture-exposed. Low-income adolescents on Medicaid are catching up to upper-income adolescents.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Most shared tables now include several people who aren't hungry. The unmedicated movement has made the long meal its sacrament: Pittsburgh's 'Long Table' Sunday suppers in Lawrenceville and Bloomfield, the Tulsa 'Bread Alone' church fasts (now ~500 congregations), and college-town potlucks where guests wear a small wheat-ear pin to say 'not on anything'. School cafeterias in districts with high adolescent use report rising food waste.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles now carry three flags: 'on', 'off' and 'unmedicated'. The third has become an identity, especially among women under 30 in college towns. Couples therapists use the 2029 anhedonia label as a shared vocabulary ('is it me or is it the dose'), and 'dose-down weekends' are common advice.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: The anhedonia label hardened the split. For clinics, payers and the public programmes, appetite is a chronic risk factor managed at $10 a month. For the unmedicated movement, appetite is evidence of being a whole person. The label is their proof text, and they quote 'reduced pleasure or interest' on placards. Most people sit in between and call it 'quiet'.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Labelled Oct 2029. Clinically meaningful anhedonia occurs in ~6.5% of users versus ~2.9% of controls, is dose-related and mostly reversible. About 30% of users report a milder 'evenness'. With ~58.7M users, the labelled excess (~3.6%) implies roughly 2.1M Americans with drug-attributable anhedonia at any time. The marketed version is the 'evenness', sold to people who are mostly not obese.
interior_life.framing: It is sold as calm. Telehealth subscriptions market low-dose generic semaglutide as 'craving freedom' and 'a quieter head', with names like Hims & Hers 'Still', Ro 'Even' and a dozen smaller apps, at $39–59 a month including the visit. FDA rules bar the generic makers from marketing it, so the companies market the service, the clinician and the 'protocol'. The FDA label calls it an adverse effect. The FTC calls the ads deceptive when they omit the warning. Subscribers call it the point.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Employer encouragement has given way to consumer purchase. Fewer employers mandate adherence; more offer a 'calm stipend' toward subscriptions as a perk. The 'steadiness' hiring preference persists informally in call centres and logistics. Productivity influencers pair microdoses with focus apps. The EEOC settled one of the two 2028 ADA charges in 2029, and the employer dropped its side-effect penalty; the other is in litigation. Sales and creative-agency managers quietly complain about 'flat' teams.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Flat' fiction has moved from literary curiosity to bestseller-list genre. Unmedicated art answers it with loud, long-form, food-heavy work: the Unmuted collective now tours, and its 'off nights' have become ticketed events in eight cities. Sportsbooks report wagering among identifiable users ~15% below non-users and have shifted marketing to the unmedicated young. Late-night bar culture keeps shrinking outside big cities.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Desire mismatch is the most common presenting complaint at couples therapy chains. The label gave people permission to blame the drug, and some do so accurately. Synchronised drug holidays around anniversaries and fertility attempts feed cycling. Some unmedicated singles say outright that they will not date users.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The unmedicated movement is a cross-partisan identity bloc without a party. MAHA-aligned state legislators, fat-acceptance groups, religious fasting networks and young progressive food activists back 'informed appetite' bills. These would require the anhedonia Medication Guide paragraph to be read aloud at adolescent starts, ban adherence conditions in Medicaid, and stop telehealth 'calm' advertising. Texas and Pennsylvania passed the advertising limits; California passed its adherence-premium ban in 2029. Opponents of the Medicare benefit cite the label. Turnout effects remain unmeasurable, and the 'sedated electorate' claim is still unsupported.

state.regulatory_posture: The FDA is fast on approvals (retatrutide, survodutide and oral amycretin all cleared this window) and has turned firmer on safety communication: the class anhedonia warning and the generic pen-labelling guidance. With the FTC, it has issued about 40 warning letters on 'calm' marketing but has no authority over telehealth service advertising beyond deception law. The import alert stays in place and now targets peptide 'research chemicals'.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: The state is now the largest payer. The Metabolic Health Access Act (Nov 2029) created a generic-only Medicare Part D obesity benefit with a $10 copay, a 90% federal Medicaid match, and HRSA free provision for uninsured adults under 250% FPL (arithmetic in access.public_coverage). There is no mandate to take the drugs. Agencies talked up the benefit as a public-health achievement, while MAHA-aligned officials at the same department kept issuing 'food first' guidance.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The Medicare benefit requires annual weight and, for enrollees 65+, a baseline DXA, but not adherence. Two state Medicaid programmes still tie continued coverage to adherence and BMI progress. Five state employee plans keep monitored tracks. Telehealth 'calm' subscriptions collect mood-tracking data under consumer terms, outside HIPAA; that is now a privacy-advocacy target.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE added generic semaglutide for weight management in 2030 because the cost became trivial. The Army made supervised oral use for near-standard recruits permanent. DOT still has not ruled on drivers using the drugs to cut drinking, and trucking firms now fund generic prescriptions for drivers outright.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Indian API makers (Biocon, Dr. Reddy's, Sun) supply much of US generic semaglutide, the same molecule that CBP was seizing in 2028. US biosecurity procurement rules keep Chinese peptide API out of federal-programme supply but not out of the gray market. Denmark faces a Novo-driven slowdown, and Danish politicians who spent years attacking US prices now lobby Washington over the Medicare formulary's generic-only rule.

events.event: FDA adds class warning for 'reduced pleasure or interest (anhedonia)' to all incretin labels, citing ~6.5% vs ~2.9% prevalence in a 61,000-patient postmarketing study

Congress passes Metabolic Health Access Act in year-end package: generic-only Medicare obesity benefit at $10 copay, 90% Medicaid match, HRSA free provision for uninsured; CBO scores $46B over ten years
Under May 2029 Paragraph IV settlement, FDA-approved generic semaglutide launches alongside Novo's authorised generic; cash prices reach $39–59 a month by summer
FTC and FDA send warning letters to 14 telehealth firms marketing low-dose generic semaglutide subscriptions as 'calm' and 'craving freedom' without disclosing the anhedonia warning
Unmedicated movement's 'Long Table' marches draw ~40,000 in Pittsburgh and Harrisburg as Pennsylvania passes limits on telehealth 'calm' advertising and adolescent consent rules
FDA approves Novo's oral amycretin after head-to-head trial finds it non-inferior to tirzepatide (~20.6% vs ~21.0% weight loss at 72 weeks)

open_tensions: The state is now the default payer for a drug that carries a labelled ~1-in-28 excess risk of anhedonia, and two state Medicaid programmes still require patients to keep taking it to keep coverage. The unmedicated movement and the label's own wording are now arguments in legislatures.

Generic prices dissolved the price gap but left a gap in efficacy. Public programmes pay for 15% semaglutide in a pen, while the insured get 21–26% tirzepatide, retatrutide or oral amycretin. Tirzepatide's 2031–32 exclusivity cliff and Medicare's generic-only rule set up the next formulary fight.

A generic-only Medicare benefit has put ~4.5M more older adults on semaglutide during the years of highest fracture risk, under a DXA requirement many pharmacies' kiosks are only beginning to meet. The absolute fracture count is expected to rise in the 2031–32 data.

'Calm' is sold to people who are mostly not obese, through telehealth services the FDA cannot regulate as drug promotion. Medicaid EPSDT has roughly doubled adolescent use, and the first pediatric bone data are not due until 2031.

prose.headline: The $39 Quiet: Generics Arrive, Washington Pays, and the Label Finally Admits What Users Felt
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 more than one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, close to fifty-nine million people. More than a quarter of adults have tried one. The biggest change in two years is not who takes these drugs. It is that the price stopped being the story. In January, under a patent settlement Novo Nordisk signed the previous spring, generic semaglutide reached American pharmacies a year or two before anyone expected. Novo launched its own authorised generic the same week. By summer a month of pens cost thirty-nine to fifty-nine dollars at Costco or Amazon, less than a gym membership. The Wegovy box still shows a list price of $1,349. It is a museum label now.

Cheap made it politically possible to pay for. Late in 2029, Congress folded a Medicare obesity benefit into a year-end package. The benefit covers only generics, with a ten-dollar copay. The same law offered states a ninety percent federal match to cover generic incretins in Medicaid and paid community health centres to hand the drug out free to uninsured adults near the poverty line. It scored at a fraction of the bill that had killed the Medicare pilot in 2027. Thirty-four states and Washington, DC now cover the drugs through Medicaid. Public programmes pay for more prescriptions than employers do, and most new starts this year were publicly paid. The poorest third of the country, which had been the least medicated, is catching up quickly.

The needle barrier also fell for the strongest drugs. In September the FDA approved Novo's oral amycretin, a daily pill that matched tirzepatide head to head. But a generic semaglutide tablet needs about seventy-five times as much drug as a weekly shot. So public programmes buy the pen, and the pill is what insured people take. The gap between rich and poor is no longer about whether you can get the drug. It is about which one. Public patients lose about fifteen percent of their weight on generic semaglutide after a ten-minute visit. Patients with good coverage lose twenty to twenty-six percent on Lilly's tirzepatide or retatrutide, or on the new pill, with protein coaching and a trainer.

The agency that approved the pill had already done something users had waited years for. In October 2029 it put a warning for reduced pleasure or interest on every incretin label, with a number attached. About six and a half percent of users develop clinically meaningful anhedonia, against roughly three percent of comparable non-users. Mostly it lifts when the dose comes down. Every pharmacy bag now carries a paragraph about it. Telehealth companies read the same evidence differently. They sell low-dose generic subscriptions for calm, focus and craving freedom, mostly to people who are not obese, and market the service because they cannot legally market the drug. Regulators send warning letters, and subscriptions grow anyway.

The resistance has become an identity. Young women in college towns wear a small wheat-ear pin that means 'not on anything'. In Pittsburgh, Sunday long-table suppers in Lawrenceville sell out weeks ahead, and in August tens of thousands marched there and in Harrisburg. Pennsylvania then limited 'calm' advertising and tightened consent rules for teenagers. Church fasting networks, fat-acceptance groups and MAHA-aligned legislators march under the same banners and agree on almost nothing else. Their placards quote the FDA label.

The industries keep adjusting. Snack dollar sales finally slipped as lower-income households, the industry's most loyal buyers, began taking the drugs. Spirits are down a tenth since 2025. Novo is cutting jobs while Lilly prospers. Older Americans are the newest large group of users, and pharmacies are installing bone scanners because their hips are the next number to watch. From the outside, the country looks healthier and quieter. Most of it is.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Rosa Delgado, sixty-one, works as a home health aide in Pittsburgh. She picks up her pen at the Giant Eagle on Penn Avenue on her way to Mr. Kowalczyk's. The pharmacist staples the bag shut over the folded Medication Guide. Rosa has read it before. 'Reduced pleasure or interest.' Medicaid pays the whole cost now. Last year she ordered vials from a website with a Mumbai address.

Mr. Kowalczyk is eighty-four and on the new Medicare benefit. He shows her the DXA printout from the CVS kiosk like a report card. 'Osteopenia,' he says, proud of the word. She helps him do his chair squats and logs ten on the clipboard.

At noon she eats half a turkey sandwich in the car and wraps the rest for later. She doesn't eat it later either.

Her phone buzzes twice. The first is the plan's refill reminder. The second is from her daughter Gabi: 'Sunday 6pm. You're coming. Don't dose Saturday.'

On Sunday the supper is in a Lawrenceville storefront with one long table and forty strangers. Gabi cooks in an apron with a wheat-ear pin. Bread arrives, then beans, then a pork shoulder that takes four people to carry. The room is very loud. A man across from Rosa laughs until he coughs.

Rosa eats a little of everything. She can taste it, and it's good. She notices she's watching people enjoy it the way she watches Mr. Kowalczyk's squats, counting.

'Well?' Gabi asks, flushed, at the door.

'It was lovely,' Rosa says, and means it. She'll dose Wednesday.
